SECURITY EDUCATION
NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION
THIRD TERM

PRIMARY 6

TOPIC - TYPES OF CRIME
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Crime
3. Lesson Evaluation and Weekly Assessment (Test)
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. define crime.
2. state types of crime in the society.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
The pupils can define a crime.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of chart or video showing crime scene.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.

5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
A crime is an illegal act or behaviour that is punishable by law or the authority.  An illegal act or behaviour such are stealing, robbery, raping, false confession, kidnapping, cultism, terrorism, etc. are forbidden by law.
The person that commits a crime is called a criminal.
TYPES OF CRIME
There are different types of crime,
1. Violent crime
2. Property crime
3. White-collar crime
4. Organized crime
5. Consensual or victimless crime
6. Political crime
LESSON 2 - TYPES OF CRIME
VIOLENT CRIME
Violet crime is a physical attack on people during crime scene. 1It is the used physical force or weapon to hurt, harm or caused injury to another person.
Examples of violet crimes are homicide, manslaughter, rape, sexual assault, robbery, domestic violence, terrorism, kidnapping, etc.
PROPERTY CRIME
Property crime is a crime that destroy other people’s properties or take away their properties. This type of crime is not a crime on people but a crime on their properties.
Examples of property crime are burglary, larceny, motor vehicle theft, and arson.
WHITE COLLAR CRIME
White collar crime is not violent in nature. It is the used of legal job, position, occupation, office, etc. to commit crimes such as corruption, scam, all kinds of fraud, money laundering, etc.
ORGANIZED CRIME
Organized crimes are not cheap and easy crimes. They are crimes committed by the wealthy and powerful people. This kind of crime is well planned, controlled and carried out on a large scale.
Examples of organized crime are oil theft, oil bunker, banditry, looting, illegal mining, human trafficking, etc.
CONSENSUAL OR VICTIMLESS CRIME
Victimless crime is a crime with no direct victim or harm on any other person except the person or people that involved.
Examples of victimless crime are gambling, drug use, pornography, prostitution, homosexuality, etc.
POLITICAL CRIME
Political crimes are crimes committed by the government or against the government. It is motivated by political goals.
LESSON 3 - WEEKLY ASSESSMENT (TEST)
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. Teacher revises the previous lesson based on the pupil’s related knowledge or understanding.
2. Teacher organizes the pupils into two or more groups depends on the size of the class.
3. Teacher displays chart showing different crime scenes.
4. Teacher lets the pupils in group to examine the chart and discuss.
Pupil’s Activities - The pupils identify and discuss the content of the chart.
5. Teacher uses the pupil’s relevant responses to introduce the lesson - Meaning and Types of Crime.
Pupil’s Activities - The pupils pay attention to the lesson introduction to understand the concept of the lesson.
6. Teacher leads a class discussion on the meaning and types of crime.
Pupil’s Activities - The pupils participate actively in the class discussion.
7. Teacher uses charts showing different types of crime to further explain each type of crime using appropriate examples.
Pupil’s Activities - The pupils uses the charts to discuss different types of crime using relevant examples.
8. Teacher summarizes the lesson on the board with appropriate lesson evaluation.
Pupil’s Activities - The pupils participate actively in the summary of the lesson by responding correctly to most of the questions and write as instructed.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (ROBBERY): MEANING, CAUSES AND WAYS TO PREVENT ROBBERY
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 5 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 3
THEME - NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION
PREVIOUS LESSON - Threats to Personal Security (Rape): Meaning and Causes of Rape | Primary 5 (Basic 5) Third Term Week 2 Security Education
TOPIC - THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (ROBBERY)
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Causes of Robbery
3. Ways of Preventing Robbery
4. Effects of Robbery
5. Safety Rules for Children
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of robbery.
2. Identify causes or factors that may contribute to robbery.
3. Mention at least five ways of preventing robbery.
4. State the effects of robbery on individuals and society.
5. Demonstrate safe actions to take when faced with a robbery or suspicious situation.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about threats to personal security, including rape, and ways of protecting themselves from unsafe or dangerous situations.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about robbery as another threat to personal security, its causes, its effects, and ways of preventing or reducing the risk of robbery.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures showing safe and unsafe security situations
2. Charts showing robbery prevention measures
3. Flashcards
4. Security Education textbook
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People may face different threats to their personal security, including theft and robbery. Robbery can involve the use of force, threats, or violence to take another person’s money or property.
People can reduce the risk of robbery by being alert, securing their homes and belongings, avoiding unsafe places, and reporting suspicious activities to trusted adults or appropriate authorities.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and causes of robbery, its effects, and ways of preventing or reducing the risk of robbery.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF ROBBERY
Robbery is the act of taking another person’s money, property, or belongings by using violence, threats, or force.
Robbery is a serious crime that can cause injury, fear, loss of property, and emotional distress.
CAUSES OF ROBBERY
Some factors that may contribute to robbery include:
1. Poverty and Unemployment - Lack of employment and financial difficulties may contribute to some people engaging in criminal activities.
2. Greed - Some people may desire to obtain money or valuable possessions through illegal means.
3. Peer Pressure - Some individuals, especially young people, may be influenced by friends or groups to participate in criminal activities.
4. Drug and Substance Abuse - The misuse of drugs or other substances can contribute to risky and criminal behaviour.
5. Poor Security - Inadequate security in homes, businesses, or public places may make it easier for criminals to commit robbery.
6. Lack of Proper Supervision - Places or situations without adequate supervision may provide opportunities for criminals to operate.
LESSON 2 - WAYS TO PREVENT ROBBERY
People can reduce the risk of robbery by following these safety measures:
1. Avoid Displaying Valuable Items - People should avoid openly displaying large amounts of money, expensive jewellery, phones, or other valuable possessions.
2. Be Alert - People should pay attention to their surroundings, especially when walking in unfamiliar or isolated places.
3. Avoid Walking Alone in Unsafe Places - Children should avoid isolated areas and should stay with trusted adults or groups when necessary.
4. Keep Doors and Windows Secure - Homes and other buildings should have properly secured doors and windows.
5. Keep Valuables Safe - Money and valuable items should be kept in secure places.
6. Report Suspicious Activities - Suspicious activities should be reported to parents, teachers, community leaders, security personnel, or the appropriate authorities.
7. Do Not Resist During a Robbery - If confronted by a robber, personal safety should come first. People should avoid unnecessary confrontation and should seek help when it is safe to do so.
8. Avoid Sharing Security Information - People should not disclose passwords, security codes, home security arrangements, or other sensitive information to strangers.
LESSON 3 - EFFECTS OF ROBBERY
Robbery can:
1. Cause physical injuries.
2. Lead to loss of property and money.
3. Create fear and anxiety.
3. Damage businesses and homes.
5. Cause emotional distress.
6. Create insecurity in the community.
SAFETY RULES FOR CHILDREN
Children should:
1. Stay close to trusted adults.
2. Avoid isolated places.
3. Never follow strangers.
4. Avoid displaying expensive items unnecessarily.
5. Inform a trusted adult when they notice something suspicious.
6. Never confront or chase suspected robbers.
7. Move to a safe place and seek help during an emergency.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Robbery is a serious crime involving the use of force, threats, or violence to take another person’s property.
- People can reduce the risk of robbery by being alert, securing their homes and belongings, avoiding unsafe places, and reporting suspicious activities to trusted adults or appropriate authorities.
- Personal safety should always come first.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Robbery is the act of taking another person’s property by using _______.
A. kindness
B. force or threats
C. cooperation
D. friendship
2. Which of the following may contribute to robbery?
A. Good security
B. Respect
C. Honesty
D. Greed
3. Which of the following can help prevent robbery?
A. Displaying large amounts of money
B. Walking alone in isolated places
C. Being alert to one’s surroundings
D. Sharing security information with strangers
4. If a child notices suspicious activity, the child should _______.
A. confront the person
B. chase the person
C. tell a trusted adult
D. keep it secret
5. During a robbery, a person’s first priority should be _______.
A. protecting personal safety
B. chasing the robber
C. fighting the robber
D. recovering property immediately
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Robbery involves taking a person’s property by using force, threats, or _______.
7. _______ may contribute to some people engaging in criminal activities.
8. People should avoid openly displaying expensive or _______ possessions.
9. Suspicious activities should be reported to a trusted adult or appropriate _______.
10. Children should avoid walking alone in _______ places.
C. True or False
11. Robbery is a serious crime. _______
12. Displaying large amounts of money openly can increase the risk of becoming a target. _______
13. Children should confront suspected robbers. _______
14. Keeping doors and windows secure can help prevent robbery. _______
15. Personal safety should come before property during a robbery. _______
D. Matching
16. Robbery - A. Paying attention to one’s surroundings
17. Secure doors and windows - B. Taking property through force or threats
18. Alertness - C. Strong desire for money or possessions
19. Greed - D. Behaviour that may indicate danger or wrongdoing
20. Suspicious activity - E. A measure that helps protect a home
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. D 3. C 4. C 5. A
6. Violence
7. Poverty
8. Valuable
9. Authority
10. Isolated
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. True
16. Robbery - B. Taking property through force or threats
17. Secure doors and windows - E. A measure that helps protect a home
18. Alertness - A. Paying attention to one’s surroundings
19. Greed - C. Strong desire for money or possessions
20. Suspicious activity - D. Behaviour that may indicate danger or wrongdoing
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that robbery is the act of taking another person’s money, property, or belongings through force, threats, or violence.
They learned that factors that may contribute to robbery include:
- Poverty and unemployment
- Greed
- Peer pressure
- Drug and substance abuse
- Poor security
- Lack of proper supervision
Pupils also learned that robbery can cause physical injuries, loss of property, fear, emotional distress, and insecurity in the community.
They learned ways to prevent or reduce the risk of robbery, including:
- Being alert to their surroundings.
- Avoiding isolated and unsafe places.
- Keeping doors and windows secure.
- Keeping valuable items in safe places.
- Avoiding unnecessary display of valuables.
- Reporting suspicious activities to trusted adults or appropriate authorities.
- Avoiding confrontation with suspected robbers.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What is robbery?
- What should you do if you see something suspicious?
- Why should we protect our homes and personal belongings?
- What should you do if you are faced with a dangerous situation?
The teacher explains that robbery is a serious threat to personal security and that people should learn how to reduce the risk and stay safe.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention some safety measures they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Robbery
The teacher explains that robbery is the act of taking another person’s money, property, or belongings by using force, threats, or violence.
The teacher explains that robbery is a crime that can cause injury, fear, loss of property, and emotional distress.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of robbery in their own words.
Step 3: Causes of Robbery
The teacher explains some factors that may contribute to robbery:
- Poverty and unemployment
- Greed
- Peer pressure
- Drug and substance abuse
- Poor security
- Lack of proper supervision
The teacher explains that these factors do not excuse criminal behaviour, and that responsibility for robbery belongs to the person who commits the crime.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention factors that may contribute to robbery.
Step 4: Effects of Robbery
The teacher explains that robbery can:
- Cause physical injuries.
- Lead to loss of money and property.
- Create fear and anxiety.
- Cause emotional distress.
- Damage homes and businesses.
- Create insecurity in the community.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the effects of robbery on individuals and society.
Step 5: Avoiding the Display of Valuables
The teacher explains that people should avoid openly displaying large amounts of money, expensive jewellery, phones, or other valuable possessions unnecessarily.
The teacher explains that children should also avoid showing valuable items to strangers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention valuable items that should be kept safely.
Step 6: Being Alert and Avoiding Unsafe Places
The teacher explains that people should pay attention to their surroundings, especially when travelling or walking in unfamiliar areas.
- Children should avoid isolated places and should stay with trusted adults or groups when necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention safe places and explain why isolated areas should be avoided.
Step 7: Securing Homes and Belongings
The teacher explains that people can reduce the risk of robbery by:
- Keeping doors and windows properly secured.
- Keeping valuable items in safe places.
- Avoiding sharing security information with strangers.
- Informing trusted adults about suspicious activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify ways of keeping their homes and belongings safe.
Step 8: What to Do During a Robbery
The teacher explains that if a person is confronted by a robber, personal safety should come first.
- People should avoid unnecessary confrontation, fighting, or chasing the robber. They should move to a safe place and seek help when it is safe to do so.
- Children should immediately inform a trusted adult or appropriate authority.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state what they should do if they encounter a dangerous situation.
Step 9: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into groups.
- Group 1: Mention five factors that may contribute to robbery.
- Group 2: List five ways of preventing or reducing the risk of robbery.
- Group 3: Mention five safety rules to follow during or after a robbery.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 10: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning, causes, and effects of robbery and discusses ways of preventing or reducing the risk of robbery.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 11: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of robbery, its causes, effects, and prevention.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Threats to Personal Security (Cultism): Meaning of Cultism, Causes of Cultism and Why Cultism Is a Threat to Personal Security | Primary 5 (Basic 5) Third Term Week 4 Security Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is robbery?
2. Mention five factors that may contribute to robbery.
3. List five ways of preventing or reducing the risk of robbery.
4. State five effects of robbery on individuals or society.
5. What should a child do after noticing suspicious activity?
6. Why should a person avoid confronting a robber?

topics.content:
THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (RAPE): MEANING AND CAUSES OF RAPE
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 5 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 2
THEME - NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION
PREVIOUS LESSON - Identification of Different Security Information II: More Security Information and Their Functions | Primary 5 (Basic 5) Second Term Week 9 Security Education
TOPIC - THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (RAPE)
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Causes and Risk Factors Associated with Rape
3. Effects of Rape
4. How Children can stay Safe and Important Safety Rules
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of rape in simple terms.
2, Identify some causes or factors associated with rape.
3. Explain why rape is a serious threat to personal security.
4. Identify trusted adults or appropriate authorities to report sexual abuse to.
5. State ways of protecting themselves from unsafe or abusive situations.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about personal security, unsafe situations, and ways of protecting themselves from danger.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about rape as a serious threat to personal security, factors that may contribute to its occurrence, and the importance of reporting sexual abuse to a trusted adult or appropriate authority.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Child-friendly safety posters
2. Pictures showing safe and unsafe situations
3. Flashcards showing personal safety rules
4. Security Education textbook
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every child has the right to feel safe and protected from harm. Children may sometimes find themselves in situations where another person attempts to violate their personal boundaries or safety.
Rape is a serious sexual offence involving sexual activity without consent. It is never the victim’s fault, and children should know that they have the right to say no to inappropriate behaviour and seek help from a trusted adult.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of rape, factors associated with its occurrence, its effects on personal security, and the importance of reporting sexual abuse to a trusted adult or appropriate authority.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF RAPE
Rape is a serious sexual offence in which a person is forced, threatened, or otherwise made to engage in sexual activity without their consent.
Rape is never the victim’s fault. Every person has the right to control what happens to their body, and children must be protected from all forms of sexual abuse.
CAUSES AND RISK FACTORS ASSOCIATED WITH RAPE
Rape is caused by the actions and choices of the offender, not by the victim’s clothing, behaviour, or location. Some factors that can contribute to the occurrence of rape include:
1. Abuse of Power or Authority - A person may misuse a position of authority or trust to sexually exploit another person.
2. Lack of Respect for Consent - Some offenders ignore or deliberately violate another person’s right to say no.
3. Violence and Aggression - A person who uses violence, threats, or intimidation may force another person into sexual activity.
4. Exploitation of Vulnerable People - Offenders may target people who are vulnerable, dependent, isolated, or unable to protect themselves.
5. Unsafe or Unsupervised Situations - Situations where children or vulnerable people are left alone with an unsafe person can increase opportunities for abuse.
6. Harmful Social Attitudes - Attitudes that encourage the control, objectification, or disrespect of others can contribute to sexual violence.
LESSON 2 - EFFECTS OF RAPE
Rape can have serious effects on a victim, including:
1. Fear and emotional distress.
2. Physical injuries.
3. Loss of trust.
4. Difficulty concentrating at school or work.
5. Feelings of shame or confusion.
5. Long-term emotional and psychological difficulties.
LESSON 3 - HOW CHILDREN CAN STAY SAFER
Children should:
1. Know that their body belongs to them.
2. Understand that they can say “No” to unwanted touching.
3. Avoid keeping secrets about inappropriate touching or sexual behaviour.
4. Tell a trusted adult if someone makes them feel unsafe.
5. Move away from a situation that feels dangerous when possible.
6. Never blame themselves if someone abuses them.
7. Seek help immediately from a trusted adult or appropriate authority.
IMPORTANT SAFETY MESSAGE
- Children should understand that no one has the right to force them into sexual activity or touch their private parts inappropriately.
- If a child experiences or witnesses sexual abuse, they should tell a trusted adult and seek help.
- The child should not be blamed for the abuse.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Rape is a serious violation of a person’s rights and personal security.
- It involves sexual activity without consent and can cause serious physical and emotional harm.
- Children should be taught about personal boundaries, consent, trusted adults, and how to report unsafe or abusive behaviour.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Rape is a serious form of ______.
A. cooperation
B. sexual abuse
C. friendship
D. sexual abuse
2. Rape occurs when sexual activity takes place without a person’s ______.
A. permission or consent
B. education
C. clothing
D. friendship
3. Which of the following can contribute to the occurrence of rape?
A. Respect for others
B. Abuse of power
C. Peaceful dialogue
D. Kindness
4. If a child experiences inappropriate sexual behaviour, the child should ______.
A. keep it secret
B. blame themselves
C. tell a trusted adult
D. ignore it
5. Which of the following is a trusted adult a child can report abuse to?
A. Teacher
B. Stranger
C. Unknown person online
D. Someone making threats
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Rape is a serious ______ offence.
7. Sexual activity without a person’s consent is a violation of their personal ______.
8. Abuse of ______ or authority can contribute to sexual abuse.
9. A child who experiences sexual abuse should tell a ______ adult.
10. Rape is never the ______ of the victim.
C. True or False
11. Rape is a serious threat to personal security. ______
12. A child should keep sexual abuse a secret. ______
13. Abuse of power can contribute to sexual violence. ______
14. Victims of rape should be blamed for what happened to them. ______
15. Children should report unsafe or abusive behaviour to a trusted adult. ______
D. Matching
Match each item in Column A with the correct answer in Column B.
16. Rape - A. A person who can provide help and protection
17. Consent - B. Sexual activity without consent
18. Trusted adult - C. Voluntary agreement or permission
19. Abuse of power - D. Misusing authority to harm or exploit another person
20. Sexual abuse - E. Unwanted sexual behaviour or activity
ANSWER KEY
1. D 2. A 3. B 4. C 5. A
6. Sexual
7. Security
8. Power
9. Trusted
10. Fault
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. B - Sexual activity without consent
17. C - Voluntary agreement or permission
18. A - A person who can provide help and protection
19. D - Misusing authority to harm or exploit another person
20. E - Unwanted sexual behaviour or activity
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that rape is a serious sexual offence involving sexual activity without a person’s consent. They learned that rape is a serious threat to personal security and is never the fault of the victim.
Pupils learned that factors associated with the occurrence of rape include:
- Abuse of power or authority.
- Lack of respect for consent.
- Violence, threats, or intimidation.
- Exploitation of vulnerable people.
- Unsafe or unsupervised situations.
- Harmful attitudes that encourage disrespect for others.
Pupils also learned that children should protect their personal boundaries, avoid unsafe situations where possible, and tell a trusted adult if they experience or witness sexual abuse.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What does personal security mean?
- What should you do when someone makes you feel unsafe?
- Who can you tell when you are in danger?
- Why is it important to report unsafe or abusive behaviour?
The teacher explains that every child has the right to be safe from harm and abuse. Children should understand their personal boundaries and know how to seek help when they feel unsafe.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention trusted adults they can seek help from.
Step 2: Meaning of Rape
The teacher explains that rape is a serious sexual offence involving sexual activity without a person’s consent.
The teacher emphasises that rape is never the victim’s fault and that no one has the right to force another person into sexual activity.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of rape in simple words and state that everyone has the right to personal safety and bodily boundaries.
Step 3: Abuse of Power or Authority
The teacher explains that some offenders may misuse their position of authority, trust, or responsibility to sexually exploit another person.
The teacher teaches pupils that having authority over someone does not give a person the right to violate that person’s body or boundaries.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss why people in positions of trust should protect others and never abuse their authority.
Step 4: Lack of Respect for Consent
The teacher explains that consent means freely agreeing or giving permission. Sexual activity without consent is wrong.
The teacher teaches pupils that they should tell a trusted adult if someone pressures, threatens, or attempts to involve them in inappropriate sexual behaviour.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of consent and identify appropriate actions when their boundaries are not respected.
Step 5: Violence, Threats and Exploitation
The teacher explains that violence, threats, intimidation, and exploitation of vulnerable people can be associated with sexual abuse.
The teacher emphasises that children should not obey threats to keep sexual abuse secret and should seek help from a trusted adult.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify safe actions to take when someone threatens or attempts to harm them.
Step 6: Unsafe or Unsupervised Situations
The teacher explains that children should be careful in situations where they may be isolated with someone who makes them feel unsafe.
The teacher encourages pupils to:
- Stay close to trusted people when possible.
- Move away from unsafe situations.
- Seek help when they feel threatened.
- Report inappropriate behaviour.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention ways they can respond when they feel unsafe.
Step 7: Reporting Sexual Abuse
The teacher explains that children should tell a trusted adult if they experience or witness sexual abuse.
Trusted adults may include:
- Parents or guardians
- Teachers
- Head teachers
- Responsible family members
- Appropriate authorities
The teacher emphasises that children should not blame themselves or keep abuse secret.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify trusted adults they can report to and practise saying, “I need help” when they feel unsafe.
Step 8: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into groups.
- Group 1: Mention five personal safety rules.
- Group 2: Mention five trusted adults or appropriate people a child can report sexual abuse to.
- Group 3: State five things a child should do when experiencing unsafe or abusive behaviour.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 9: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of rape, factors associated with its occurrence, the importance of personal boundaries, and the need to report sexual abuse to trusted adults.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 10: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of rape, personal safety, and appropriate ways of seeking help.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (CULTISM): MEANING OF CULTISM, CAUSES OF CULTISM AND WHY CULTISM IS A THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 5 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 4
THEME - NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION
PREVIOUS LESSON - Threats to Personal Security (Robbery): Meaning, Causes and Ways to Prevent Robbery | Primary 5 (Basic 5) Third Term Week 3 Security Education
TOPIC - THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY (CULTISM)
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Causes of Cultism
3. Why Cultism is a Threat to Personal Security
4. Effects of Cultism and How to Avoid Cultism
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of cultism.
2. Identify factors that may influence people to join cult groups.
3. Mention at least five causes of cultism.
4. Explain why cultism is a threat to personal security.
5. State ways of avoiding cultism and resisting peer pressure.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about threats to personal security, including rape and robbery, their causes, effects, and ways of staying safe.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about cultism, factors that may influence people to join cult groups, the dangers of cultism, and ways children can avoid harmful groups and peer pressure.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures showing positive and negative peer influence
2. Charts showing the dangers of cultism
3. Flashcards showing personal security rules
4. Pictures of children participating in positive group activities
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People belong to different groups at home, in school, and in their communities. Some groups are formed for positive purposes, while others may be secretive and harmful.
Cultism involves belonging to a secret or closely controlled group whose activities or beliefs may be harmful to individuals or society. Cultism can expose people to violence, threats, crime, and other dangers.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and causes of cultism, why cultism is a threat to personal security, and ways of avoiding cult groups and resisting harmful peer pressure.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF CULTISM
Cultism is the practice of belonging to a secret or closely controlled group whose activities, beliefs, or rules may be harmful to individuals or society.
Cult groups may operate secretly and may encourage members to engage in activities that can cause violence, intimidation, crime, or other forms of harm.
CAUSES OF CULTISM
Some factors that may influence people to join cult groups include:
1. Peer Pressure - Some people may join cult groups because their friends or peers encourage or pressure them to do so.
2. Desire for Protection - Some individuals may wrongly believe that belonging to a cult group will protect them from threats or enemies.
3. Desire for Power and Recognition - Some people may be attracted to cult groups because they want to feel powerful, important, or respected.
4. Bad Influence - Negative influence from friends, older people, or criminal groups may encourage individuals to become involved in cultism.
5. Lack of Proper Guidance - Young people who lack proper parental or adult guidance may be more vulnerable to harmful influences.
6. Desire for Wealth or Material Benefits - Some people may be attracted to groups that promise money, possessions, or other benefits.
7. Curiosity - Some individuals may become interested in secret groups because they are curious about their activities or promises.
LESSON 2 - WHY CULTISM IS A THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY
Cultism can threaten personal security because it may involve:
1. Violence and fighting.
2. Threats and intimidation.
3. Injury or loss of life.
4. Destruction of property.
5. Criminal activities.
6. Fear and insecurity.
7. Bullying and harassment.
8. Conflict within schools and communities.
9. Pressure to participate in harmful activities.
EFFECTS OF CULTISM
Cultism can negatively affect individuals and society by:
1. Causing injuries and death.
2. Destroying friendships and family relationships.
3. Disrupting education.
4. Leading to criminal behaviour.
5. Creating fear in schools and communities.
6. Causing destruction of property.
7. Preventing peaceful living.
8. Bringing legal consequences to those involved.
LESSON 3 - HOW TO AVOID CULTISM
Children can protect themselves by:
1. Avoiding secret or harmful groups.
2. Choosing friends carefully.
3. Saying “No” to peer pressure.
4. Seeking guidance from parents, teachers, and other trusted adults.
5. Reporting threats or attempts to recruit them.
6. Avoiding violent activities and bad influences.
7. Participating in positive school and community activities.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Cultism involves belonging to secret or closely controlled groups whose activities may be harmful to individuals and society.
- Peer pressure, desire for power, bad influence, lack of guidance, and curiosity are some factors that may encourage involvement in cultism.
- Cultism is a threat to personal security because it can lead to violence, intimidation, injury, crime, fear, and loss of life.
- Children should avoid cult groups and seek help from trusted adults when they experience pressure or threats.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Cultism is the practice of belonging to a _______.
A. sports team
B. secret or harmful group
C. school club
D. family
2. Which of the following may influence a person to join a cult group?
A. Good guidance
B. Discipline
C. Respect
D. Peer pressure
3. A person may join a cult group because of a desire for _______.
A. peaceful living
B. good education
C. power and recognition
D. cooperation
4. Which of the following is a danger of cultism?
A. Violence
B. Peace
C. Friendship
D. Cooperation
5. What should a child do when pressured to join a cult group?
A. Join immediately
B. Keep it secret
C. Say no and tell a trusted adult
D. Encourage friends to join
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. _______ is one factor that may influence young people to join harmful groups.
7. Lack of proper _______ can make young people vulnerable to harmful influences.
8. Cultism can lead to violence, threats, and _______.
9. Children should choose their _______ carefully.
10. A child who is pressured to join a cult group should seek help from a _______ adult.
C. True or False
11. Cultism can be a threat to personal security. _______
12. Peer pressure can influence some people to join harmful groups. _______
13. Cultism always promotes peace and unity. _______
14. Children should report threats or attempts to recruit them to a trusted adult. _______
15. Joining a cult group is a safe way of gaining protection. _______
D. Matching
16. Cultism - A. Influence from friends to do something
17. Peer pressure - B. Belonging to a secret or harmful group
18. Violence - C. Physical force intended to cause harm
19. Trusted adult - D. A responsible person who can provide guidance and help
20. Personal security - E. Protection from danger, harm, or threats
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. D 3. C 4. A 5. C
6. Peer pressure
7. Guidance
8. Crime
9. Friends
10. Trusted
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. False
16. B - Belonging to a secret or harmful group
17. A - Influence from friends to do something
18. C - Physical force intended to cause harm
19. D - A responsible person who can provide guidance and help
20. E - Protection from danger, harm, or threats
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that cultism is the practice of belonging to a secret or closely controlled group whose activities, beliefs, or rules may be harmful to individuals or society.
They learned that factors that may influence people to join cult groups include:
- Peer pressure
- Desire for protection
- Desire for power and recognition
- Bad influence
- Lack of proper guidance
- Desire for wealth or material benefits
- Curiosity
Pupils also learned that cultism is a threat to personal security because it can lead to violence, threats, intimidation, injury, crime, destruction of property, fear, and loss of life.
They learned that children can avoid cultism by choosing friends carefully, resisting peer pressure, seeking guidance from trusted adults, avoiding harmful groups, and reporting threats or recruitment attempts.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What is a group?
- Mention some positive groups you belong to in school or at home.
- What can happen when someone joins a harmful group?
- Who can you talk to if someone pressures you to join a harmful group?
The teacher explains that people belong to different groups, but some secret or harmful groups can threaten people’s safety and wellbeing. One example is cultism.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention positive groups they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Cultism
The teacher explains that cultism is the practice of belonging to a secret or closely controlled group whose activities, beliefs, or rules may be harmful to individuals or society.
The teacher explains that cult groups may encourage violence, intimidation, crime, or other harmful activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain cultism in their own words.
Step 3: Peer Pressure
The teacher explains that peer pressure occurs when friends or people of the same age influence someone to behave in a particular way.
The teacher explains that negative peer pressure can encourage a person to join a harmful group.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of positive and negative peer pressure.
Step 4: Other Causes of Cultism
The teacher explains some factors that may influence people to join cult groups:
- Desire for protection.
- Desire for power and recognition.
- Bad influence.
- Lack of proper guidance.
- Desire for wealth or material benefits.
- Curiosity.
The teacher emphasises that these factors do not justify cultism or criminal behaviour.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention factors that may influence people to join harmful groups.
Step 5: Why Cultism Is a Threat to Personal Security
The teacher explains that cultism is a threat to personal security because it may involve:
- Violence and fighting.
- Threats and intimidation.
- Injury or loss of life.
- Destruction of property.
- Criminal activities.
- Bullying and harassment.
- Fear and insecurity.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state ways cultism can threaten personal security.
Step 6: Effects of Cultism
The teacher explains that cultism can:
- Cause injury or death.
- Disrupt education.
- Destroy friendships and family relationships.
- Lead to criminal behaviour.
- Create fear in schools and communities.
- Cause destruction of property.
- Prevent peaceful living.
- Bring legal consequences.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the effects of cultism on individuals, schools, families, and communities.
Step 7: Ways to Avoid Cultism
The teacher explains that children can avoid cultism by:
- Choosing friends carefully.
- Saying “No” to harmful peer pressure.
- Avoiding secret or harmful groups.
- Seeking guidance from parents, teachers, and other trusted adults.
- Reporting threats or attempts to recruit them.
- Participating in positive school and community activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention ways of avoiding cultism and resisting negative peer pressure.
Step 8: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into three groups.
- Group 1: Mention five factors that may influence people to join cult groups.
- Group 2: State five ways cultism can threaten personal security.
- Group 3: List five ways children can avoid cultism.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 9: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of cultism, factors that may influence people to join cult groups, the dangers of cultism, and ways of avoiding cultism.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 10: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of cultism, its causes, dangers, and prevention.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

ADVANCE FEE FRAUD (419) AS A THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY:MEANING OF ADVANCE FEE FRAUD AND PREVENTIVE MEASURES AGAINST ADVANCE FEE FRAUD
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 5 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION
PREVIOUS LESSON - Threats to Personal Security (Cultism): Meaning of Cultism, Causes of Cultism and Why Cultism Is a Threat to Personal Security | Primary 5 (Basic 5) Third Term Week 4 Security Education
TOPIC - ADVANCE FEE FRAUD (419) AS A THREAT TO PERSONAL SECURITY
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Common Examples of Advance Fee Fraud (419)
3. Preventive Measures Against Advance Fee Fraud (419)
4. Effects of Advance Fee Fraud (419)
5. Safety Rules for Children
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of advance fee fraud (419).
2. Identify common examples of advance fee fraud.
3. Mention at least five ways of preventing advance fee fraud.
4. Explain why advance fee fraud is a threat to personal security.
5. State what to do when they receive a suspicious message or offer.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about threats to personal security, including robbery and cultism, and ways of protecting themselves from dangerous situations.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about advance fee fraud (419), how fraudsters deceive people, and ways of protecting themselves from fraudulent offers and requests for money or personal information.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures showing common fraud messages and fake offers
2. Charts showing ways to prevent advance fee fraud
3. Flashcards
4. Sample safe and unsafe messages
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People can be deceived by individuals who make false promises of money, jobs, scholarships, prizes, or other benefits. They may ask the victim to pay money or provide personal information before receiving the promised benefit.
This type of fraud is called advance fee fraud or 419. It is a threat to personal security because it can cause people to lose money or expose their personal information.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of advance fee fraud (419), common examples of fraudulent offers, and ways of protecting themselves from fraud.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF ADVANCE FEE FRAUD (419)
Advance fee fraud, commonly called 419, is a type of fraud where a person is tricked (deceived) into giving money or personal information in order to receive a promised benefit.
The fraudster may promise money, a job, a scholarship, a contract, or an inheritance. After the victim gives the money or information, the promised benefit may not be given.
COMMON EXAMPLES OF ADVANCE FEE FRAUD
Advance fee fraud may involve:
- Fake job offers that require payment before employment.
- Fake scholarships that require registration or processing fees.
- False promises of contracts or business opportunities.
- Fake inheritance or lottery claims.
- Messages claiming that someone has won money and must pay a fee to receive it.
- Requests for money to release a supposed package or prize.
LESSON 2 - PREVENTIVE MEASURES AGAINST ADVANCE FEE FRAUD
1. Do Not Pay Money for Suspicious Promises - Do not send money simply because someone promises you a large reward, job, scholarship, contract, or prize.
2. Verify Information - Check whether an offer is genuine before taking any action. Use official contact details and trusted sources to verify the information.
3. Do Not Share Sensitive Information - Do not give strangers your passwords, PINs, bank details, verification codes, or other private information.
4. Be Careful with Unexpected Messages - Be suspicious of unexpected emails, text messages, phone calls, or social media messages that ask for money or personal information.
5. Avoid Offers That Seem Too Good to Be True - Promises of quick and unusually large rewards should be treated with caution.
6. Ask a Trusted Adult - Children should discuss suspicious offers with their parents, guardians, teachers, or another trusted adult before responding.
7. Report Suspected Fraud - Suspected fraud should be reported to a trusted adult and the appropriate authorities.
LESSON 3 - EFFECTS OF ADVANCE FEE FRAUD
Advance fee fraud can:
1. Cause financial loss.
2. Lead to theft of personal information.
3. Cause emotional distress.
4. Destroy trust.
5. Expose victims to further fraud.
6. Create fear and insecurity.
SAFETY RULES FOR CHILDREN
Children should:
1. Never send money to strangers because of an online or phone promise.
2. Never share passwords, PINs, or verification codes.
3. Never meet an unknown person because of an online offer.
4. Tell a trusted adult about suspicious messages or offers.
5. Verify information before believing or sharing it.
6. Avoid clicking suspicious links or opening unexpected attachments.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Advance fee fraud or 419 is a form of fraud in which victims are deceived into paying money or providing valuable information in anticipation of a benefit that may never come.
- People can protect themselves by verifying offers, refusing suspicious payment requests, protecting personal information, asking trusted adults for help, and reporting suspected fraud.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Advance fee fraud is commonly called ______ in Nigeria.
A. 419
B. 911
C. 999
D. 112
2. Advance fee fraud involves tricking a person into giving ______.
A. food
B. clothes
C. books
D. money or personal information
3. Which of the following is an example of advance fee fraud?
A. A genuine school admission
B. A fake job offer that requires payment
C. A classroom activity
D. A normal bank transaction
4. Which of the following should you NOT share with strangers?
A. Your favourite colour
B. Your password or PIN
C. Your favourite subject
D. Your hobby
5. What should a child do after receiving a suspicious offer?
A. Send money immediately
B. Share it with friends
C. Tell a trusted adult
D. Reply with personal information
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Advance fee fraud is commonly known as __________ in Nigeria.
7. Fraudsters may promise victims money, jobs, scholarships, or __________.
8. People should not give their passwords or __________ to strangers.
9. Suspicious offers should be checked before taking any __________.
10. Children should report suspicious messages to a __________ adult.
C. True or False
11. Advance fee fraud is a form of fraud. ______
12. People should pay money immediately when they receive a suspicious offer. ______
13. A fake scholarship that requires payment before receiving the scholarship can be advance fee fraud. ______
14. People should protect their personal information from strangers. ______
15. Children should tell a trusted adult about suspicious offers. ______
D. Matching
16. Advance fee fraud - A. A secret number used to protect an account
17. 419 - B. A person who is deceived by a fraudster
18. Fraudster - C. Another name for advance fee fraud
19. Victim - D. A person who deceives others for illegal gain
20. PIN - E. Fraud that involves payment or information for a false promise
ANSWER KEY
1. A - 419
2. D - Money or personal information
3. B - A fake job offer that requires payment
4. B - Your password or PIN
5. C - Tell a trusted adult
6. 419
7. Contracts
8. PINs
9. Action
10. Trusted
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. True
15. True
16. E - Fraud that involves payment or information for a false promise
17. C - Another name for advance fee fraud
18. D - A person who deceives others for illegal gain
19. B - A person who is deceived by a fraudster
20. A - A secret number used to protect an account
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that advance fee fraud, commonly called 419, is a type of fraud where a person is tricked into giving money or personal information in order to receive a promised benefit.
They learned that fraudsters may make false promises of:
- Money or prizes
- Jobs
- Scholarships
- Contracts
- Inheritance
- Other valuable benefits
Pupils also learned ways of preventing advance fee fraud, including:
- Not paying money for suspicious promises.
- Verifying information before taking action.
- Keeping passwords, PINs, and other personal information private.
- Being careful with unexpected messages and offers.
- Avoiding offers that seem too good to be true.
- Asking a trusted adult for advice.
- Reporting suspected fraud to the appropriate authority.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- Have you ever received a message promising you a prize or gift?
- Should you give money to a stranger because of a promise?
- What should you do when you receive a suspicious message?
- Who can you ask for advice?
The teacher explains that some people deceive others by making false promises of money, jobs, scholarships, prizes, or other benefits. This is known as advance fee fraud or 419.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share examples of suspicious offers they may have heard about.
Step 2: Meaning of Advance Fee Fraud (419)
The teacher explains that advance fee fraud, commonly called 419, is a type of fraud where a person is tricked into giving money or personal information in order to receive a promised benefit.
The teacher explains that the promised benefit may not actually exist.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of advance fee fraud in their own words.
Step 3: Common Examples of Advance Fee Fraud
The teacher explains that fraudsters may make false promises such as:
- A fake job that requires payment before employment.
- A fake scholarship that requires a fee.
- A fake lottery or prize that requires payment to collect it.
- A false promise of an inheritance.
- A fake business contract or opportunity.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify examples of fraudulent offers.
Step 4: How Advance Fee Fraud Happens
The teacher explains that a fraudster may contact a person through a phone call, text message, email, social media, or other means.
The fraudster may ask the person to:
- Pay a fee
- Send money
- Provide a password or PIN
- Give other personal information
The teacher explains that people should not respond to such requests without verifying them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify suspicious requests that they should avoid.
Step 5: Do Not Pay for Suspicious Promises
The teacher explains that pupils should never send money because someone promises them a prize, job, scholarship, or other benefit.
The teacher emphasises that children should always tell a trusted adult before responding to suspicious offers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state what they should do when asked to pay money for an unexpected benefit.
Step 6: Protect Personal Information
The teacher explains that people should keep personal information safe.
Pupils should not share:
- Passwords
- PINs
- Bank details
- Verification codes
- Other private information
The teacher explains that such information should only be provided through safe and trusted channels when necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention information they should keep private.
Step 7: Verify Information
The teacher explains that people should verify an offer before believing or acting on it.
They should:
- Check the information using trusted sources.
- Ask a parent, guardian, teacher, or another trusted adult.
- Avoid clicking suspicious links.
- Avoid responding to unknown senders.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain how they can check whether an offer is genuine.
Step 8: Report Suspected Fraud
The teacher explains that suspicious messages or fraud attempts should be reported to a trusted adult and the appropriate authorities.
The teacher reminds pupils not to confront or threaten suspected fraudsters.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention people they can report suspicious messages or offers to.
Step 9: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into three groups.
- Group 1: Mention five examples of advance fee fraud.
- Group 2: List five ways of preventing advance fee fraud.
- Group 3: Mention five types of personal information that should be kept private.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 10: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of advance fee fraud, common examples, ways fraudsters deceive people, and measures for preventing fraud.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 11: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of advance fee fraud, its examples, and preventive measures.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES

1. Explain the meaning of punishment.
2. Identify different types of punishment.
3. Mention punishments that may be given for different offences.
4. Explain the importance of punishment in maintaining peace and order.
5. State why people should not take the law into their own hands.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about different threats to personal security, such as rape, robbery, cultism, and advance fee fraud, including their meanings, causes, effects, and preventive measures.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about punishment, types of punishment, and the importance of lawful punishment for people who commit offences.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People are expected to obey the laws and rules of society. When a person breaks a law, the person may face a lawful consequence called punishment.
Punishment helps to discourage people from committing offences, protect members of society, and maintain peace and order. However, punishment should be lawful, fair, and appropriate, and people should never take the law into their own hands.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and types of punishment, examples of lawful punishments for various offences, and the importance of punishment in promoting security and responsible behaviour.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF PUNISHMENT
Punishment is a lawful action taken against a person who breaks a rule or law.
Punishment is meant to discourage people from committing offences, encourage good behaviour, and help maintain peace and order in society.
Punishment should be lawful, fair, and appropriate to the offence. People should not take the law into their own hands.
TYPES OF PUNISHMENT
1. Imprisonment - Imprisonment is the confinement of a person in prison after being found guilty of an offence by a court.
2. Fine - A fine is money ordered by a court to be paid as punishment for an offence.
3. Community Service - Community service requires a person, as ordered by a court, to perform certain useful activities for the community.
4. Probation - Probation allows an offender to remain in the community under specific conditions and supervision instead of being sent to prison, where the law permits.
5. Warning or Reprimand - A person may receive a formal warning or reprimand for certain less serious offences, depending on the rules or law involved.
LESSON 2 - PUNISHMENT FOR VARIOUS THREATS TO PERSONAL SECURITY
Different offences may have different punishments depending on the law and circumstances of the offence.
1. Rape and sexual abuse: Serious legal offences that may result in imprisonment and other penalties prescribed by law.
2. Robbery: A serious criminal offence that may result in imprisonment and other penalties prescribed by law.
3. Cultism: Participation in unlawful cult-related activities may attract legal penalties, including imprisonment, depending on the offence and applicable law.
4. Advance fee fraud (419): Fraud offences may attract imprisonment, fines, or other penalties prescribed by law.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF PUNISHMENT
Punishment is important because it helps to:
1. Discourage people from committing offences.
2. Promote obedience to laws and rules.
3. Protect people and their property.
4. Maintain peace and order.
5. Encourage responsible behaviour.
6. Ensure that offenders are held accountable through lawful processes.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Punishment is a lawful consequence for breaking rules or laws.
- There are different types of punishment, including imprisonment, fines, community service, probation, and warnings or reprimands.
- The punishment for an offence depends on the applicable law and circumstances.
- Everyone should obey the law and report threats to personal security to the appropriate authorities.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that punishment is a lawful action taken against a person who breaks a rule or law.
They learned that types of punishment include:
- Imprisonment

- Warning or reprimand
Pupils also learned that the punishment for an offence depends on the law and circumstances of the offence. Serious offences such as rape, robbery, cult-related offences, and fraud may attract serious legal penalties.
They learned that punishment is important because it helps to:
- Discourage people from committing offences.
- Promote obedience to laws and rules.
- Protect people and their property.
- Maintain peace and order.
- Encourage responsible behaviour.
- Hold offenders accountable through lawful processes.
Pupils also learned that people should not take the law into their own hands but should report offences to the appropriate authorities.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What happens when someone breaks a school rule?
- Why do we have rules and laws?
- What can happen when a person breaks a law?
- Who is responsible for deciding lawful punishment?
The teacher explains that people are expected to obey the rules and laws of society. When a person breaks a law, the person may face a lawful consequence called punishment.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention examples of rules and consequences they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Punishment
The teacher explains that punishment is a lawful action taken against a person who breaks a rule or law.
The teacher explains that punishment is used to discourage unlawful behaviour, promote obedience to laws, and maintain peace and order.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of punishment in their own words.
Step 3: Imprisonment
The teacher explains that imprisonment is the confinement of a person in prison after being found guilty of an offence by a court.
The teacher explains that imprisonment is usually used for serious offences, according to the law.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain what imprisonment means.
Step 4: Fine
The teacher explains that a fine is money ordered by a court to be paid as punishment for an offence.
The teacher gives simple examples to help pupils understand the meaning of a fine.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of a fine and identify it as a type of punishment.
Step 5: Community Service
The teacher explains that community service requires a person, as ordered by a court, to perform useful activities for the community.
The teacher gives examples such as helping to clean or maintain approved public places, where permitted by law.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention useful activities that can benefit the community.
Step 6: Probation
The teacher explains that probation allows an offender to remain in the community under specific conditions and supervision instead of being sent to prison, where the law permits.
The teacher explains that a person on probation must obey the conditions set by the court.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain probation in simple terms.
Step 7: Warning or Reprimand
The teacher explains that for some less serious offences, a person may receive a formal warning or reprimand, depending on the applicable rules or law.
The teacher explains that a warning tells the person that the behaviour is unacceptable and should not be repeated.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state why a person may be given a warning or reprimand.
Step 8: Punishment for Various Threats to Personal Security
The teacher explains that different offences have different punishments according to the law and circumstances.
Examples include:
- Rape and sexual abuse: May attract serious legal penalties, including imprisonment.
- Robbery: May attract imprisonment and other penalties prescribed by law.
- Cult-related offences: May attract legal penalties, depending on the offence and applicable law.
- Advance fee fraud: May attract fines, imprisonment, or other penalties prescribed by law.
The teacher emphasises that only the appropriate authorities and courts can determine lawful punishment.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify examples of offences and discuss why punishment should be determined according to the law.
Step 9: Importance of Punishment
The teacher explains that punishment helps to:
- Discourage people from committing offences.
- Promote obedience to laws and rules.
- Protect people and property.
- Maintain peace and order.
- Encourage responsible behaviour.
- Hold offenders accountable through lawful processes.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the importance of punishment.
Step 10: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into three groups.
- Group 1: Mention five types of punishment.
- Group 2: State five reasons why punishment is important.
- Group 3: Match different offences with appropriate examples of lawful consequences.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 11: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning and types of punishment, examples of lawful consequences for offences, and the importance of punishment in maintaining peace and order.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 12: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of punishment, its types, and its importance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.

INTRODUCTION
Rape and unlawful cult-related activities are serious threats to personal security. They can cause injury, fear, violence, loss of life, and other harm to individuals and communities.
When a person commits an offence and is found guilty, the law may prescribe an appropriate punishment. Punishment helps to discourage crime, protect people, and promote peace and security.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the possible legal punishment for rape and unlawful cult-related activities, the importance of punishment, and why people should report offences to the appropriate authorities instead of taking the law into their own hands.
LESSON 1 - PUNISHMENT FOR RAPE
Rape is a serious sexual offence. A person found guilty of rape may receive serious punishment according to the law, which may include imprisonment and other penalties prescribed by law.
Rape is a serious crime because it violates a person’s rights and can cause physical and emotional harm.
IMPORTANCE OF PUNISHING RAPE
Punishment for rape helps to:
1. Protect people from sexual violence.
2. Discourage people from committing rape.
3. Hold offenders accountable.
4. Promote safety in society.

LESSON 2 - PUNISHMENT FOR CULTISM
Cultism involves belonging to or participating in a secret or harmful group. Where cult-related activities are unlawful, a person found guilty may face legal punishment according to the applicable law.
The punishment may depend on the particular offence committed and can include imprisonment, fines, or other penalties provided by law.
IMPORTANCE OF PUNISHING CULTISM
Punishment for unlawful cult-related activities helps to:
1. Discourage violence and criminal activities.
2. Protect individuals and communities.
3. Promote peace and security.
4. Prevent intimidation and bullying.
5. Hold offenders accountable.
IMPORTANCE OF LAWFUL PUNISHMENT
Punishment for threats to personal security should be handled through lawful procedures. People should not attack, beat, or punish suspected offenders themselves. The police, courts, and other appropriate authorities are responsible for investigating offences and applying the law.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Children are important members of every family and community. Because children are still growing and developing, they need special care, protection, and support.
Under the Child Rights Act, a child is a person under 18 years of age. Lagos State also has a Child’s Rights Law that provides protection for children and promotes their welfare and development.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the definition of a child under the Child Rights Act, the Child Rights Law in Lagos State, and how the law protects children from abuse, exploitation, discrimination, and harmful practices.
LESSON 1 - DEFINITION OF A CHILD UNDER THE CHILD RIGHTS ACT
Under the Child Rights Act (CRA) 2003, a child is a person who is under the age of 18 years.
The law provides special protection for children because they are still growing and developing.
CHILD RIGHTS LAW IN LAGOS STATE
Lagos State has laws and institutions for protecting the rights and welfare of children. The Child’s Rights Law of Lagos State provides for the protection, care, development, and welfare of children in the state.
The law helps to protect children from:
1. Abuse and neglect
2.Exploitation

4..Violence

LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF CHILD RIGHTS LAW IN LAGOS STATE

1. Protects children from abuse and exploitation.
2. Promotes the welfare and development of children.
3. Supports children’s access to education and health care.
4. Protects children from harmful practices.
5. Promotes the right of children to proper care and protection.

1. Respect parents, teachers, and other people.
2. Obey reasonable rules and laws.
3. Attend school and take their education seriously.
4. Respect the rights of other children.
5. Avoid harmful activities.
6. Report abuse or danger to a trusted adult.
ON A FINAL NOTE
- Under the Child Rights Act 2003, a child is a person under 18 years of age.
- Lagos State also has a Child’s Rights Law designed to protect children’s rights, welfare, development, and safety.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that under the Child Rights Act, a child is a person under 18 years of age.
They also learned that the Child Rights Law in Lagos State provides protection for children and promotes their welfare, development, and safety.
The law protects children from:
- Abuse and neglect
- Exploitation
- Violence
- Discrimination
- Harmful practices
- Child labour and other harmful treatment.
Pupils also learned that children have rights such as the right to education, health, care, protection, and a safe environment. They also have responsibilities, including respecting others, obeying reasonable rules, taking their education seriously, and reporting abuse or danger to a trusted adult.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- Who is a child?
- At what age does a person become an adult?
- Why do children need special protection?
- What can children do when their rights are violated?
The teacher explains that children are still growing and developing, so they need care, protection, and support. Laws have been made to protect their rights and welfare.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about children’s rights and protection.
Step 2: Definition of a Child
The teacher explains that under the Child Rights Act (CRA) 2003, a child is a person under 18 years of age.
The teacher explains that the law provides special protection for children because they are still developing.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the age limit for a child under the Child Rights Act.
Step 3: Meaning of Child Rights Law in Lagos State
The teacher explains that the Child’s Rights Law of Lagos State is a law that provides for the protection, care, development, and welfare of children in Lagos State.
The law helps to ensure that children are treated properly and protected from harmful treatment.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of Child Rights Law in their own words.
Step 4: Protection from Abuse and Neglect
The teacher explains that children should be protected from physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, as well as neglect.
The teacher explains that children should tell a trusted adult when they experience or witness abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify trusted adults they can report abuse or danger to.
Step 5: Protection from Exploitation and Child Labour
The teacher explains that children should be protected from exploitation and harmful forms of child labour.
The teacher explains that children should have time for education, rest, play, and healthy development.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention activities that may be harmful to children’s education or development.
Step 6: Protection from Harmful Practices and Discrimination
The teacher explains that children should be protected from harmful practices, violence, and unfair treatment.
The teacher explains that every child deserves respect and protection regardless of their background or circumstances.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of fair and respectful treatment of children.
Step 7: Rights of Children
The teacher reminds pupils of some important rights of children:
- Right to life.
- Right to a name and identity.
- Right to education.
- Right to health.
- Right to parental care and protection.
- Right to freedom from discrimination.
- Right to protection from abuse and exploitation.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention and identify different rights of children.
Step 8: Importance of Child Rights Law in Lagos State
The teacher explains that the law is important because it:
- Protects children from abuse and exploitation.
- Promotes children’s welfare and development.
- Supports children’s education and health.
- Protects children from harmful practices.
- Promotes the safety and dignity of children.
- Provides legal protection when children’s rights are violated.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the importance of Child Rights Law.
Step 9: Responsibilities of Children
The teacher explains that children also have responsibilities. They should:
- Respect parents, teachers, and other people.
- Obey reasonable rules and laws.
- Respect the rights of other children.
- Take their education seriously.
- Avoid harmful activities.
- Report abuse or danger to a trusted adult.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention their responsibilities at home, in school, and in the community.
Step 10: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into three groups.
- Group 1: State the definition of a child under the Child Rights Act.
- Group 2: Mention five protections provided for children under child rights law.
- Group 3: List five responsibilities of children.
Each group presents its answers to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers.
Step 11: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the definition of a child under the Child Rights Act and explains the purpose and importance of the Child Rights Law in Lagos State.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise what they have learned.
Step 12: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of the definition of a child, Child Rights Law in Lagos State, children’s rights, and their responsibilities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

CHILD’S RIGHT LAW: MEANING OF LAW, MEANING OF RIGHT AND CHILD’S RIGHTS ACT IN NIGERIA
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 5 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 9
THEME - NATIONAL VALUES EDUCATION

LEARNING AREA

2. Meaning of Law
3. Meaning and Examples of Rights
4. Meaning of Child Rights, Child Rights Act in Nigeria and Importance

6. Responsibilities of Children

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of law.
2. Explain the meaning of a right.
3. Define child rights.
4. State the purpose of the Child Rights Act in Nigeria.
5. Mention at least five rights of children protected by law.
6. State some responsibilities of children in the family, school, and society.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about personal security, threats to personal security, and the importance of laws and lawful punishment in protecting people.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about the meaning of law, the meaning of rights, child rights, and the Child Rights Act in Nigeria, which provides protection for children.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Chart showing children’s rights
2. Pictures of children in school, hospital, and family settings
3. Flashcards
4. Nigerian Child Rights Act textbook/materials
5. Security Education textbook
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
